title: Supplemental Oxygen
summary: Connect cabin pressure, oxygen delivery, and pilot performance before symptoms become a decision-making problem.
objectives: Explain why altitude lowers useful oxygen availability while the atmospheric percentage remains nearly constant.
Apply §91.211 using cabin pressure altitude and the correct occupant category.
Distinguish hypoxia from hyperventilation without delaying protective action.
Evaluate oxygen devices, duration, servicing, and monitoring as one system.

sections.title: The percentage stays near 21%; pressure falls
sections.body:
The oxygen fraction of ordinary air remains approximately 21 percent as altitude increases through normal aviation operating altitudes. The problem is falling total pressure. Oxygen partial pressure falls with it, reducing the pressure available to move oxygen from the lungs into the blood.

A pressurized cabin changes the environment your body experiences. The relevant physiological variable is cabin pressure altitude, the standard-atmosphere altitude corresponding to the cabin’s pressure. In an unpressurized airplane, that generally follows outside pressure altitude. A healthy-looking cabin, a low workload, or a normal indicated aircraft altitude does not independently prove that occupants have adequate oxygen.

PO2=xO2×Pambient

For dry ambient air at 10.0 psi, a 21 percent oxygen fraction gives 0.21 × 10.0 = 2.10 psi oxygen partial pressure. Humidification and gas exchange change conditions inside the respiratory system; this calculation describes the dry ambient mixture.
sections.deep: Why: Breathing more vigorously cannot fully replace the pressure gradient lost at high altitude. Supplemental oxygen raises the inhaled oxygen fraction, while pressurization raises the pressure of the whole breathing environment. At sufficiently high altitude, even a high oxygen fraction may require a properly approved pressure-demand system. The aircraft and oxygen equipment limitations determine the usable envelope.

sections.title: Recognize the failure in the delivery chain
sections.body:
Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen at the tissues. Hypoxic hypoxia can result from altitude or inadequate inhaled oxygen. Hypemic hypoxia involves insufficient oxygen-carrying capability, as with carbon monoxide exposure. Stagnant hypoxia involves inadequate circulation. Histotoxic hypoxia occurs when tissues cannot use the oxygen delivered, as with certain substances.

Symptoms can include poor judgment, euphoria, slowed responses, headache, visual changes, and impaired coordination. They are variable and may be missed by the affected pilot. Treat an unexpected change in performance or behavior at altitude as meaningful evidence. Protect breathing, verify oxygen delivery, and follow the aircraft’s applicable emergency and descent procedures.
sections.deep: Why: Confidence can rise while reasoning deteriorates, so feeling comfortable is a weak safeguard. Time of useful consciousness describes the time available for purposeful protective action, not a guaranteed interval until fainting. Altitude, exertion, individual condition, and decompression rate change that interval. Prepare equipment and decisions before exposure rather than planning to diagnose yourself after symptoms become obvious.

sections.title: The legal minimum uses cabin pressure altitude
sections.body:
Cabin pressure altitudeGeneral §91.211(a) requirement
Above 12,500 through 14,000 ftRequired minimum flight crew use oxygen for the portion exceeding 30 minutes in this band.
Above 14,000 ftRequired minimum flight crew use oxygen throughout the exposure.
Above 15,000 ftProvide supplemental oxygen for every occupant.

Those are minimum requirements, not a guarantee of unimpaired performance below the threshold. Earlier use can be prudent, particularly at night or with individual susceptibility. Do not substitute aircraft flight altitude for cabin pressure altitude when applying this table.
sections.deep: Apply it: At a 13,500-foot cabin pressure altitude for 45 minutes, the required crew needs oxygen for the portion beyond 30 minutes. At 14,500 feet, required crew use is continuous. Above 15,000 feet, all occupants must have oxygen provided; the wording for occupants differs from the crew-use requirement. Aircraft, operator, and other applicable requirements can be more restrictive.

sections.title: Rapid breathing can lower carbon dioxide
sections.body:
Hyperventilation is excessive ventilation relative to the body’s needs. It removes too much carbon dioxide and can cause tingling, dizziness, confusion, or muscle symptoms. It is not simply “too much oxygen.” Stress can start a cycle in which uncomfortable sensations provoke even faster breathing.

Hypoxia and hyperventilation can produce similar symptoms and can occur together. At altitude, do not assume anxiety is the whole explanation or remove needed oxygen. Follow the aircraft’s guidance, establish effective oxygen delivery when indicated, and consciously control breathing rate and depth. Evaluate the flight condition and use the appropriate descent or emergency procedure.
sections.deep: Why: Oxygen supply and carbon-dioxide removal are related but different physiological problems. Correcting breathing technique does not repair a disconnected oxygen hose, and increasing oxygen does not by itself explain every symptom. Teach students to protect oxygenation first when hypoxia is possible, then evaluate equipment, breathing, and other causes without delaying aircraft control.

sections.title: Match the whole system to the mission
sections.body:
A continuous-flow system supplies a set flow, a demand system delivers oxygen during inhalation, and pulse-demand equipment meters a pulse when it detects a breath. Pressure-demand equipment can supply oxygen under positive pressure. The delivery device, regulator, oxygen source, and aircraft installation must be compatible and approved for the intended operation.

Check the equipment’s altitude limits rather than assigning every system of a named type one universal ceiling. A nasal cannula is normally limited to 18,000 feet, and a mask may be required sooner by the approved equipment. Confirm fit, connections, settings, flow indications, available supply, and enough duration for contingencies. Brief passengers before they need the equipment.
sections.deep: Why: Oxygen remaining in a cylinder does not prove that a usable quantity reaches a person. A disconnected line, unsuitable flow setting, blocked cannula, or failure to trigger pulse delivery can defeat an otherwise full system. Use the manufacturer’s duration information with the actual number of users, altitude, and delivery settings. A generic pressure reading is not a complete endurance calculation.

sections.title: Monitor performance and handle oxygen safely
sections.body:
Use the specified aviation oxygen supply and servicing procedures. Keep oxygen equipment free of oil, grease, ignition sources, and incompatible materials. Oxygen accelerates combustion; it does not need to be a fuel itself to create a severe fire hazard. Secure cylinders and protect valves and lines as the manufacturer requires.

A pulse oximeter can help identify a changing trend, but it is a supplement to equipment checks, symptoms, and judgment. Cold fingers, poor circulation, motion, and other factors can impair readings. A reassuring number does not prove the oxygen system is working correctly or rule out every cause of incapacitation. Respond to a concerning person or trend rather than waiting for one magic display value.
sections.deep: Apply it: Before a night mountain crossing, evaluate oxygen duration for a diversion as well as the planned cruise. Put monitoring equipment where it can be used without distracting from flying. Recheck supply and delivery after altitude or device changes. The useful question is whether each person receives adequate oxygen for the actual flight, not merely whether oxygen equipment is aboard.

teachBack: Explain altitude hypoxia without saying that the percentage of oxygen falls.
Apply the oxygen rules to a 45-minute exposure at 13,500 feet cabin pressure altitude.
Demonstrate the difference between oxygen supply, delivery, and monitoring.
takeaways: Use cabin pressure altitude for the general oxygen rule.
The first crew-use band ends at 14,000 feet, not 14,500.
Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and can coexist with hypoxia.
Equipment limitations and delivery checks matter as much as having a cylinder.

quiz.question: For dry ambient air, take total pressure as 10.0 psi and the oxygen fraction as 21%. What is the oxygen partial pressure?
options: 0.21 psi
2.10 psi
4.70 psi
10.0 psi
feedback: 0.21 is the oxygen fraction expressed as a decimal. Multiply it by the total pressure to obtain a partial pressure.
Oxygen partial pressure is 0.21 × 10.0 psi = 2.10 psi. A constant oxygen fraction can therefore accompany falling oxygen pressure.
4.70 psi is the difference between a 14.7 psi sea-level reference and the stated 10.0 psi total pressure. It is not the oxygen partial pressure.
10.0 psi is the total pressure of all gases in the mixture. Oxygen contributes only its fraction of that total.
quiz.hint: For a gas mixture, multiply the gas fraction, written as a decimal, by the total pressure.

quiz.question: An unpressurized airplane remains at a cabin pressure altitude of 13,500 feet for 45 minutes. Under the general rule, when must the required minimum crew use oxygen?
options: Only after the airplane climbs above 15,000 feet.
For all 45 minutes because every exposure above 12,500 feet requires immediate use.
For the 15-minute portion exceeding 30 minutes in the band.
Never, because 13,500 feet is below 14,000 feet.
feedback: Above 15,000 feet adds an all-occupant provision; it does not remove the lower crew requirement.
The first crew-use band includes a 30-minute duration condition.
The required portion is 45 minus 30, or 15 minutes.
The duration condition applies above 12,500 through 14,000 feet.
quiz.hint: Subtract the allowed duration in this altitude band from the actual exposure.

quiz.question: At a cabin pressure altitude of 15,500 feet, which statement matches the general oxygen rule?
options: Passengers are required by this provision to wear oxygen continuously, but crew need none.
Only the pilot needs oxygen available, with no use requirement.
The rule applies only to the airplane’s indicated altitude.
Required minimum crew must use oxygen, and oxygen must be provided for every occupant.
feedback: The rule requires crew use and specifies provision for all occupants; it does not use the same wording for both groups.
Crew use is required above 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude.
Cabin pressure altitude is the relevant altitude for the general rule.
The crew-use requirement and all-occupant provision both apply at this cabin altitude.
quiz.hint: Read the crew-use and occupant-provision requirements separately.

quiz.question: What directly explains the symptoms of hyperventilation?
options: Excessive ventilation lowers carbon dioxide below the body’s needs.
A fixed 21-percent oxygen concentration is poisonous.
The cylinder contains too much pressure for any regulator.
All rapid breathing proves there is no hypoxia.
feedback: Excessive carbon-dioxide removal is the defining mechanism.
Ordinary atmospheric oxygen concentration does not define hyperventilation.
Cylinder pressure is handled by the regulator and is not the physiological definition.
Hypoxia and hyperventilation can occur together.
quiz.hint: Consider which gas is removed too rapidly.

quiz.question: A cylinder is full, but its user is becoming confused at altitude. What is the best assessment?
options: A full cylinder proves the person is adequately oxygenated.
Oxygen is never useful once symptoms appear.
Supply pressure alone does not establish delivery; protect breathing and follow the applicable emergency procedure.
The person should remove oxygen to see whether anxiety improves.
feedback: Pressure in the source does not confirm the regulator, line, or interface is delivering usable oxygen.
Prompt effective oxygen and the applicable response can be essential.
A complete system check distinguishes available supply from effective delivery while protective action proceeds.
Removing needed oxygen can worsen hypoxia.
quiz.hint: Trace oxygen from the source to the person.

quiz.question: A pulse oximeter shows a reassuring value while a pilot has concerning symptoms. What should the student conclude?
options: The symptoms can be ignored.
The reading is only one piece of evidence and does not rule out every hazard.
The oxygen system no longer needs a preflight check.
The device replaces the aircraft’s emergency guidance.
feedback: Concerning performance or symptoms still require attention.
Readings have limitations and must be interpreted alongside the person, equipment, and flight conditions.
Monitoring does not replace equipment inspection and delivery checks.
A monitoring device is not an approved aircraft emergency procedure.
quiz.hint: A measurement supports judgment rather than replacing it.
